knownIssues: Team comms may have provided information the demo cannot show (callouts, sound cues, teammates' kill positions).
The historical line is not assumed to be correct; it only records what this team did.
Sightings come from the demo's spotted flag, which can register enemies a player never consciously noticed.
Detected by a heuristic; not yet reviewed by a human CS2 reviewer.
Man-advantage shift: kills leave several defensible follow-ups (trade, hold, rotate); the detector does not judge which is best.
The follow-up information arrives less than 2 s before the next kill, leaving almost no time to react.
The follow-up is the first material change the demo shows 3-25 s later; teams may have learned of it earlier through comms.

Follow-up reaction window is only 0.11 s: in the source round the situation changed again almost at once, so the responses may not be meaningfully playable. Confirm the window is long enough or author a different follow-up.

Follow-up qualities are a proposed matrix, one cell per locked main action and line now: the value of the line now after the update, minus a switching cost (10 within the same posture, 20 one step, 30 between passive and active). A reviewer should check each row: when staying with the locked line is coherent, when changing is justified, and whether the new information really supports a reversal.

The option set (actions, qualifiers, follow-up responses) is a template for this situation family, not derived from the demo; a reviewer must confirm every option is playable on this map at this moment and that no defensible line is missing.

The debrief reasoning (whyItWorks, cost, assumption, breaksWhen, strongestAlternative, counterfactual, evidence explanations, principle) is templated per situation family and needs human tactical review.

Rubric ratings, evidence points and follow-up qualities are heuristic priors (see editorial.notes), not tactical judgements; time thresholds (defuse duration + 7 s, 25 s comfortable) are unreviewed assumptions.

debrief.whyItWorks: When most positions are unknown and the clock is long, information converts the execute from a guess into a read. Here, 2 players faced 3 with about 78 seconds left.
debrief.cost: It spends round clock, which limits the later options.
debrief.assumption: There is enough clock left to act on whatever the information shows.
debrief.breaksWhen: The clock runs down before the information is used, so the team has to execute blind anyway.

evidenceReview.explanation: Two defenders could not be placed. Unaccounted-for opponents are the main risk to any committed plan and the main reason to gather information.
The round clock stood near 78 seconds. The round clock bounds how long any plan can take.
It was 2 players against 3. The head count sets how many duels the team can lose and still carry out its plan.
The confirmed position of one defender in Palace Interior was about 2 seconds old. A sighting narrows where contact is likely, but its value falls quickly with age.
The team had no utility left. The utility left sets how much of the plan can be forced rather than hoped for.

debrief.followupReview: The follow-up was judged against the line you locked. The update did not overturn the strongest line, so staying with it scored best ("Keep playing slowly for information"). Changing course earned the value of the new line less the time and position a switch costs, so correcting a weaker call still scored well, while abandoning a sound one or holding on to a weak one did not.
debrief.strongestAlternative: The closest alternative was to commit to an execute now, spending options at once for a plant before the clock runs low.

counterfactual.changedFact: The round clock is under half a minute.
counterfactual.effect: Gathering information no longer fits, and committing at once becomes stronger.
